name: DMM Pinto Pulley Prusik Set
title: DMM Pinto Pulley Prusik Set for Arborists
meta: The DMM Pinto pulley prusik set pairs a compact pulley with a hitch cord loop for tending slack, small haul systems, and simple rope tools on the tree job.
tagline: A compact DMM pulley paired with a prusik loop for hitch tending and small haul systems.
summary: The DMM Pinto pulley prusik set combines a small, efficient pulley with a matching prusik loop, so you have the two pieces most climbers reach for when they build a hitch-tending setup or a quick mechanical advantage. It is a tidy way to add a pulley and hitch to a climbing kit in one purchase.
highlights: DMM Pinto pulley paired with a prusik loop
Pulley tends slack on a friction hitch
Also useful for small haul and retrieval systems
Compact enough to live on a saddle loop
One purchase covers both pieces

p: On a moving rope system the pulley sits below your hitch so you can pull slack through with one hand as you climb. The Pinto's side plates swing open to load the rope mid-line, and the prusik loop gives you a grab point you can set anywhere on the line. Together they make a clean, repeatable setup.

Off the climbing line, the same two pieces make a fast progress-capture point in a small mechanical advantage system: tensioning a pull line, lifting a hung limb a few inches, or snugging a tag line. Keep these setups light; heavy rigging belongs on gear built for those loads.

Check that the prusik cord diameter suits your host rope. A hitch cord that is too thin for the rope can grab too hard, and one that is too close in diameter may slip. Test any new combination low before you trust it at height.

Before each use, spin the sheave and confirm it turns freely, check the side plates for cracks or burrs, and look over the cord for glazing, cuts, and stiff or flattened spots near the hitch. Retire the cord at the first sign of heat damage. See more options in our hitch cord and split tails section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is the Pinto pulley used for in tree work?
faq.a: Mostly as a hitch-tending pulley under a friction hitch, and as a small pulley in light haul or tensioning systems.

faq.q: Does the prusik cord need replacing more often than the pulley?
faq.a: Usually yes. Hitch cord wears from heat and abrasion and should be retired when it glazes, stiffens, or shows cuts, while the pulley lasts much longer with basic care.

name: Sirius 8mm Loop Prusik with Aluminum Ring
title: Sirius 8mm Loop Prusik with Aluminum Ring
h1: Sirius 8mm Loop Prusik with Aluminum Ring
meta: The Sirius 8mm loop prusik with aluminum ring gives climbers a ready-made hitch cord with a ring for a clean, low-friction tie-in on rope tools and lanyards.
tagline: An 8 mm sewn-style prusik loop with an aluminum ring for hitch and adjuster setups.
summary: The Sirius 8mm loop prusik with ring is a ready-made hitch loop with an aluminum ring captured at one end, so a carabiner or a rope tool can connect to a smooth bearing surface instead of directly onto cord. It suits climbers who want a quick, tidy hitch on a lanyard or a backup on a climbing line.
highlights: 8 mm hitch cord formed into a loop
Aluminum ring for a smooth connection point
Reduces cord wear where the carabiner sits
Handy for lanyard adjusters and backup hitches
Ready to tie, no splicing needed

body.h: Where a ring loop prusik fits
p: A loop prusik is the simplest hitch there is: wrap it around the host rope, pass it through itself, and clip in. Adding an aluminum ring gives the carabiner a round, smooth surface to ride on, which spreads the load and cuts down on the cord wear you see when a carabiner sits directly on the loop.

Climbers use these as adjusters on a rope lanyard, as a backup hitch while they set up, or as a grab point when building a quick haul. An 8 mm cord holds well on many 11 to 13 mm arborist lines, but the bite changes with rope construction, so test it low on your own rope before you rely on it.

Because the ring is already in place, there is nothing to splice or sew. Keep a spare loop on the saddle so you can swap out a glazed adjuster mid-job or add a quick backup while you reset a tie-in point.

Inspect the cord for glazing, cuts, and hard or flattened sections, and look at the ring for nicks or grooves worn by the carabiner. A hitch that has slipped under load should be retired, because the heat can damage the fibers inside. Compare other cords in our hitch cord section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Why add a ring to a prusik loop?
faq.a: The ring gives the carabiner a smooth, round bearing point, which reduces cord wear and helps the loop sit neatly when clipped.

faq.q: Will an 8 mm loop work on my climbing rope?
faq.a: It works on many 11 to 13 mm arborist ropes, but grip varies by rope. Tie it low, load test it, and follow the rope and cord manufacturers' guidance.

name: Yale Bee Line Loop Prusik with Aluminum Ring
title: Yale Bee Line Loop Prusik with Aluminum Ring
h1: Yale Bee Line Loop Prusik with Aluminum Ring
meta: The Yale Bee Line loop prusik is an 8mm hitch cord loop with an aluminum ring for lanyard adjusters, backup hitches, and quick grab points on climbing lines.
tagline: Yale's heat-resistant 8 mm Bee Line hitch cord in a ready loop with an aluminum ring.
summary: The Yale Bee Line loop prusik puts Yale's well-known 8 mm Bee Line hitch cord into a closed loop with an aluminum ring, ready to tie on a lanyard or climbing line. Bee Line is built to handle the heat a friction hitch makes, which is why so many climbers use it for adjusters and hitches.
highlights: Made from Yale Bee Line 8 mm hitch cord
Cord built to resist hitch heat
Aluminum ring for a smooth carabiner connection
Good for lanyard adjusters and backup hitches
Ready to use out of the package

p: Bee Line has a heat-resistant core with a polyester cover, which helps it hold up to the friction a hitch generates when you descend or adjust under load. The cover has a firm hand that grips host rope well without feeling grabby once it is broken in.

As a ring loop it is quick to use. Tie a prusik or similar hitch on a rope lanyard as an adjuster, or set it on a climbing line as a backup while you rig your system. The ring keeps the carabiner from sawing on the cord and makes the loop easier to clip and unclip with gloves on.
Grip depends on the host rope. Test the hitch on your own lanyard or climbing line close to the ground before you trust it aloft.

Many climbers keep two or three of these loops on the saddle: one as a lanyard adjuster, one as a spare, and one for building a quick haul or a backup on a rigging line when the ground crew needs a hand.

Look for glazing, cuts, stiff spots, and pulled cover yarns, and check the ring for wear grooves. Retire any loop that has slipped hard under load. More hitch cords are in our hitch cord and split tails category.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is Yale Bee Line used for?
faq.a: It is an 8 mm hitch cord commonly used for friction hitches, prusik loops, and lanyard adjusters in tree climbing.

faq.q: How long does a Bee Line prusik last?
faq.a: It depends on how hard you use it. Inspect it before each climb and retire it when it glazes, stiffens, or shows cuts or core damage.

name: Edelrid Talon Replacement Cuff System
title: Edelrid Talon Replacement Cuff System for Spurs
meta: Edelrid Talon replacement cuffs restore the upper pads and straps on Talon climbing spurs, so worn cuffs can be swapped without replacing the whole set.
tagline: Replacement upper cuffs and straps for Edelrid Talon climbing spurs.
summary: Edelrid Talon replacement cuffs let you renew the upper cuff and strap system on a pair of Talon spurs once the padding has packed down or the straps are worn. Swapping cuffs is far cheaper than a new set of spurs when the shanks and gaffs are still in good shape.
highlights: Replacement cuff system for Edelrid Talon spurs
Restores support and comfort on worn spurs
Cheaper than replacing a full spur set
Keeps your fitted shanks and gaffs in service

p: Cuffs take a beating. Sweat, sap, and rubbing against bark break down padding and stretch straps, and a cuff that has packed flat no longer spreads load across your calf. You notice it as rubbing, a shank that rotates when you set a gaff, or sore shins after a removal day.

If the shanks are straight and the gaffs are sharp and within the manufacturer's wear limits, new cuffs bring the spurs back to a good working fit. Confirm you have Talon spurs before ordering, since cuff systems are model specific.

Fresh cuffs also make the spurs safer to use. A cuff that holds the shank firmly against the leg helps each gaff go in straight and stay set, which matters most when you are tired late in a long removal and your footwork starts to slip.

Follow Edelrid's instructions to remove the old cuffs and install the new ones, and make sure every fastener is secure before you climb. Adjust strap height so the top of the shank sits just below the knee without pressing into it. Find gaffs and other spare parts in our replacement gaffs and parts section.

Spurs are for removals and rescue, not pruning live trees. Inspect cuffs, straps, shanks, and gaffs before every use, and climb on spurs only after proper training and with a lanyard and climbing line rigged to the standard.

faq.q: Will Talon cuffs fit other spur models?
faq.a: Treat them as Talon-specific. Check the manufacturer's fitment guidance before trying them on any other spur.

faq.q: How do I know my spur cuffs are worn out?
faq.a: Packed-down padding, stretched or frayed straps, cracked buckles, and a shank that shifts on your leg are all signs it is time for new cuffs.

name: Speed Line Kit with Snap Hooks
title: Speed Line Kit with Snap Hooks for Brush Removal
h1: Speed Line Kit with Snap Hooks
meta: A speed line kit with snap hooks lets tree crews zip brush down a tensioned line to a drop zone. See what goes in the kit and how a speedline setup works.
tagline: A speedline setup for sending brush down a tensioned rope to a clear drop zone.
summary: A speed line kit with snap hooks gives a crew the parts to rig a tensioned line from the tree to a drop zone and send cut brush down it, clear of roofs, fences, and gardens. Snap hooks clip each piece of brush onto the line quickly, so the climber keeps cutting while the ground crew clears.
highlights: Moves brush over obstacles to a clear drop zone
Snap hooks for fast clip-on of each piece
Speeds up removals in tight yards
Cuts down on ground damage and cleanup
Works with standard rigging anchors and tensioning

p: The line runs from an anchor high in the tree to a low anchor at the drop zone, usually a stout tree or a vehicle-safe ground anchor, and is tensioned so loads slide down instead of sagging into whatever you are protecting. The climber clips a snap hook onto the butt of each limb, hooks it over the line, and makes the cut. Gravity does the rest.

Line angle and tension are the whole game. Too flat and brush stalls halfway; too steep and pieces arrive fast. A tag line on bigger pieces and a clear landing area with a ground worker standing off to the side keep it controlled. Keep pieces small; a speedline is for brush and light wood, not heavy rigging.

Anchor points carry far more load than the brush weight once the line is tensioned, so pick sound anchors and do not over-tension with mechanical advantage. Keep everyone out from under the line and the landing zone while it is running. Compare complete setups in our rigging kits.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What can you send down a speedline?
faq.a: Brush and small, light wood. Heavy wood needs a proper rigging system with a lowering device, not a speedline.

faq.q: How tight should a speedline be?
faq.a: Tight enough that pieces travel without dragging, but not so tight that you overload anchors. Use a modest mechanical advantage and stay within the ratings of every component.

name: 1/2" Husky Bull Rope Rigging Rope
title: 1/2 Inch Husky Bull Rope Rigging Rope
meta: Husky Bull Rope in 1/2 inch is a double braid rigging rope for light rigging, limb lowering, and pruning work. Learn how to size it and care for it.
tagline: A 1/2 in double braid bull rope for light rigging, limb lowering, and pruning work.
summary: Husky Bull Rope in 1/2 inch is a double braid rigging line made for lowering wood on tree removals, with a firm braid that runs well through blocks and lowering devices. The 1/2 inch size is light enough to carry up the tree and quick to handle on smaller pieces.
highlights: Double braid rigging rope construction
1/2 in diameter
Firm braid that runs well through blocks
Spliceable for eyes and slings
Sold in common rigging lengths

body.h: Picking the right bull rope size
p: Bull rope is the workhorse line on a removal: tied to the piece, run through a block or a natural crotch, and controlled from a lowering device at the base. The 1/2 inch size suits light rigging, limb lowering, and pruning work. Size the rope to the heaviest piece you plan to catch, not the average one, and remember that letting a piece run before you catch it multiplies the load.

Match your hardware to the rope. Blocks, pulleys, and lowering devices list the rope diameters they accept, and a rope that is too big for a sheave will wear quickly and lose strength. Double braid holds an eye splice well, so it is common to have a spliced eye in one end for a running bowline-free tie.

Keep rigging line out of saw oil and fuel, stored dry and out of sunlight. Run it through your hands after each job and look for cuts, glazing from a hot lowering device, crushed spots, and core showing through the cover. Retire rope that has caught a shock load near its limit. See other lines in our rigging rope section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What jobs is 1/2 inch bull rope good for?
faq.a: It suits light rigging, limb lowering, and pruning work. Check the manufacturer's strength rating and size up when pieces get heavier or you expect dynamic loads.

faq.q: How do I tell when rigging rope is worn out?
faq.a: Look for cuts, glazing, flat or stiff sections, exposed core, and fuzzing that goes deep into the braid. When in doubt, retire it.

name: 5/8" Mammoth Rigging Line
title: 5/8 Inch Mammoth Rigging Line for Tree Removal
meta: Mammoth rigging line in 5/8 inch is a heavy-duty arborist lowering rope for everyday removals. Learn how to match it to blocks and devices and when to retire.
tagline: A 5/8 in rigging line for everyday lowering on tree removals.
summary: Mammoth rigging line in 5/8 inch is a lowering rope for removal work, sized for the mid-weight wood most crews handle day to day. At 5/8 inch it runs through common arborist blocks and lowering devices and still carries easily up the tree.
highlights: 5/8 in rigging line for removal work
Runs through common arborist blocks and devices
Suits mid-weight wood and limb lowering
Easy to carry and handle on the ground

p: Five-eighths is the size many crews default to. It is big enough for most limbs and moderate trunk sections and small enough that a climber can manage it without a fight. Pair it with a block and a lowering device rated for 5/8 inch rope, and keep the heaviest wood for a bigger line.

Rigging loads are about more than the weight of the piece. A piece that falls before the rope catches it, or a hard stop at the base, can put several times its weight on the line and the anchor. Let the rope run a little to soften the catch, and keep your drops short.
Check the manufacturer's strength rating and working load guidance for this line before you size it to a job.

Store it dry and away from fuel, oil, and sunlight. Before and after each job, look along the full length for cuts, glazed or melted spots, flattened sections, and exposed core. Compare other options in our rigging rope section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: Is 5/8 inch rigging rope big enough for removals?
faq.a: For many limbs and moderate sections, yes. Heavier wood calls for a larger rope and hardware sized to match.

faq.q: Can I use rigging line for climbing?
faq.a: No. Climbing requires rope rated and sold for life support. Keep rigging line for rigging.

name: Sterling Kraken Rigging Line 3/4" x 200'
title: Sterling Kraken Rigging Line, 3/4 in x 200 ft
meta: Sterling Kraken rigging line in 3/4 inch by 200 feet is built for heavy arborist rigging on big removals. See how to size it, match hardware, and care for it.
tagline: A 3/4 in x 200 ft rigging line from Sterling for heavy removal work.
summary: Sterling Kraken rigging line is a heavy-duty arborist rope, and this 3/4 inch by 200 foot length is sized for big wood and tall removals. It gives you the length to rig from high in a large tree and the diameter to handle heavy pieces with the right block and lowering device.
highlights: Heavy-duty 3/4 in rigging line
200 ft length for tall trees and long runs
Made by Sterling Rope
Pairs with large blocks and lowering devices
Built for big removal work

p: A 3/4 inch line is for the days when wood gets heavy: big leaders, trunk wood, and pieces you would not trust to a 5/8 inch rope. The 200 foot length gives enough to reach from a high block to a lowering device at the base with plenty left to work with, even on tall trees.

Heavy rope needs heavy hardware. Pair it with a block, sling, and lowering device rated for 3/4 inch line and for the forces you expect, and keep the anchor sound. A big line does not make a weak anchor any stronger.
Check Sterling's published ratings and working load guidance before you size it to a specific job.
Long heavy rope is also heavy to carry, so most crews set it up with a light line first and haul the rigging line into position rather than climbing with it.

Long, heavy rope rewards good handling. Flake it into a bag rather than coiling it tight, keep it away from fuel and saw oil, and look over its full length for cuts, glazing, and crushed spots after each job. Compare other sizes in our rigging rope section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: When should I move up to 3/4 inch rigging rope?
faq.a: When the wood you are lowering is too heavy for your 5/8 inch line and hardware, or when you expect large dynamic loads on a removal.

faq.q: Why buy a 200 foot length?
faq.a: It gives enough rope to rig from high anchors on tall trees and still reach the lowering device with working tails.

name: Teufelberger Bomber Line 1/2" x 150'
title: Teufelberger Bomber Line 1/2 Inch x 150 ft
meta: Teufelberger Bomber Line in 1/2 inch by 150 feet is a light rigging rope for limb lowering and small removals. See how it is used and how to care for it.
tagline: A 1/2 in x 150 ft Teufelberger rigging line for light lowering work.
summary: Teufelberger Bomber Line in 1/2 inch by 150 feet is a light rigging rope for lowering limbs and small wood on pruning and removal jobs. It is easy to carry aloft and quick to tie, which makes it a good second line on the truck.
highlights: 1/2 in rigging line from Teufelberger
150 ft length for most residential trees
Light enough to carry up the tree
Good for limb lowering and small removals

body.h: What a 1/2 inch line is for
p: A light rigging line earns its spot on pruning jobs and small removals, where pieces are manageable and you want a rope you can tie fast and pull without a crew. Use it to lower limbs over roofs and gardens, as a tag line, or as a pull line when felling small trees.

Know where the size stops. Heavier wood, long drops, and pieces that will be caught hard need a bigger rope and hardware rated for those loads. Match pulleys and lowering devices to 1/2 inch rope so the line runs smoothly and wears evenly.
Check Teufelberger's ratings and guidance before sizing it to a particular piece.

A 150 foot length covers most residential trees with enough tail for the ground worker. It also packs into a small rope bag, so it can ride along on pruning jobs where you might not expect to rig at all.

Keep it clean and dry, away from fuel and saw oil. Inspect along the full length for cuts, glazing, and flat spots, and retire it after a severe shock load. More lines are in our rigging rope section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: Is 1/2 inch rope strong enough for rigging?
faq.a: For light limbs and small wood, yes, within the manufacturer's ratings. Move to a larger rope for heavier pieces.

faq.q: Can Bomber Line be used as a pull line?
faq.a: Yes, many crews use a light rigging line to pull small trees over during felling. Keep everyone clear of the fall zone.

name: CMI Rigging Block for 1/2 in Rope
title: CMI Rigging Block for 1/2 Inch Rope
h1: CMI Rigging Block for 1/2 in Rope
meta: The CMI rigging block for 1/2 inch rope redirects light rigging lines on pruning and removal jobs. See how to hang it, match rope size, and inspect it.
tagline: A rigging block sized for 1/2 in rope for light lowering work.
summary: The CMI rigging block for 1/2 inch rope is a pulley block used to redirect the line from the piece to a lowering device at the base. Using a block instead of a natural crotch reduces friction on the tree and wear on the rope.
highlights: Sized for 1/2 in rigging rope
Redirects line with less friction than a natural crotch
Hangs from a sling on a sound anchor
Reduces rope and bark wear
Made by CMI

p: Hang the block from a sling choked or girth-hitched around a sound anchor above the work. The rigging line runs through the sheave down to a lowering device at the base, where the ground worker controls the descent. Because the sheave turns, the line runs freely and the ground worker gets consistent, predictable friction from the device.

Remember that the block and anchor see roughly double the load on the rope, since the line pulls from both sides. Choose a sling and anchor that can handle that, and keep drops short to limit shock loads.

A small block is easy to carry up on the saddle, so you can set it as you go rather than sending it up on a line. That makes it a good fit for pruning jobs where you lower a handful of limbs over a roof, garden, or fence, then move on to the next tree.

Before each use, check the side plates for cracks or bending, confirm the sheave spins smoothly without wobble, and look for grooves worn by rope. Use only rope within the block's listed diameter. See larger options in our rigging blocks section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: Why use a rigging block instead of a natural crotch?
faq.a: A block reduces friction and rope wear, protects the tree, and gives the ground worker more consistent control from the lowering device.

faq.q: Can I run larger rope through a 1/2 inch block?
faq.a: No. Use only rope within the diameter range the manufacturer lists for the block.

name: CMI RP145 Arborist Block
title: CMI RP145 Arborist Rigging Block
meta: The CMI RP145 arborist block redirects rigging lines on removals with less friction than a natural crotch. See how it hangs and what to check before each job.
tagline: CMI's arborist rigging block for redirecting lowering lines on removals.
summary: The CMI RP145 arborist block is a rigging block made to hang from a sling and redirect a lowering line on tree removals. It replaces a natural crotch with a turning sheave, which saves the rope, protects the tree, and gives the ground crew smoother control.
highlights: Rigging block built for arborist lowering
Hangs from a sling on a sound anchor
Turning sheave saves rope and bark
Smoother control for the ground worker
Made by CMI

p: Set the block on a sling above the piece you are removing, run the rigging line through the sheave, and take it down to a lowering device at the base. With the block carrying the redirect, the ground worker controls the descent with the device instead of fighting crotch friction.

The anchor and block take roughly twice the load on the rope because the line pulls from both sides. Size slings and anchors to that, and choose a rope that fits the sheave as listed by CMI. Check CMI's ratings for this model before you size it to a job.
Placement matters as much as the block itself. Hang it above the piece and as close to the trunk as the work allows, so the load hangs in line with the stem and the anchor is not levered sideways.

Look for cracks, bent side plates, a loose axle, and grooves worn into the sheave. Spin the sheave by hand and make sure it runs smoothly. Retire a block that has been dropped from height or shock loaded beyond its rating. Compare other blocks in our rigging blocks.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What rope does the CMI RP145 take?
faq.a: Check CMI's listing for the RP145 and use rope within the stated diameter range.

faq.q: How do I hang a rigging block?
faq.a: Most crews use a rated sling girth hitched or choked around a sound anchor, with the block clipped or threaded on as the manufacturer allows.

body.h: Heavy rigging with the Impact Block
p: On big removals, the redirect point takes the most punishment. The block sees roughly twice the line load because the rope pulls from both sides, and a piece that drops before the catch adds more. A large block built for impact loading gives you margin where you need it most.

Pair it with rope inside DMM's listed diameter range, a sling rated for the load, and a lowering device sized to match. Keep drops short, let the rope run a little to soften the catch, and choose sound anchors. Check DMM's published ratings for the large size before planning a lift.

Larger blocks are heavier, so most climbers send them up on a line once the anchor sling is set rather than wearing them while climbing. Plan the setup before you go up so the block, sling, and lowering device are matched and ready.

Before every job, check the side plates for cracks or bending, the axle and fasteners for looseness, and the sheave for smooth rotation and wear grooves. Retire it after a fall onto a hard surface or an overload. See other sizes in our rigging blocks.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: When do I need a large rigging block?
faq.a: When you are lowering heavy wood or expect high dynamic loads, and your rope size calls for a bigger sheave.

faq.q: Does the block take double the rope load?

name: DMM Bat X-Small Rigging Plate (Orange)
title: DMM Bat X-Small Rigging Plate, Orange
meta: The DMM Bat X-Small rigging plate gives climbers and riggers a compact multi-point anchor for organizing carabiners, pulleys, and lines in a tidy system.
tagline: A compact DMM rigging plate for organizing connectors at an anchor.
summary: The DMM Bat X-Small rigging plate is a compact aluminum plate that gives you several connection holes at one point, so carabiners, pulleys, and rope tools can hang side by side without stacking on one another. In tree work it keeps anchors, retrievable setups, and small haul systems neat and easy to read.
highlights: Compact multi-hole rigging plate
Keeps carabiners from cross-loading in a pile
Neat anchor for climbing and light rigging systems
Bright orange for easy spotting
Made by DMM

p: Stack three carabiners on one anchor sling and they twist, bind, and cross-load. A rigging plate gives each connector its own hole, spread out and easy to see. Climbers use small plates at a base anchor, on a canopy anchor for a stationary rope system, or to hang a pulley and a hitch side by side in a small haul.

The X-Small size is meant for compact, lighter setups. It is not a heavy rigging component for catching big wood. Check DMM's listed strength for this plate and keep the whole system within the lowest-rated part.

A small plate also makes rope rescue setups easier to build and check, because every connector is visible at a glance. Keep it on the saddle or in the rescue kit so it is there when you need to organize a busy anchor quickly.

Look for cracks, deep scratches, and sharp edges worn into the holes by carabiners, and retire a plate that has been dropped onto rock or concrete from height. Load connectors in the holes along the plate's intended axis. See more hardware in our blocks and hardware section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: Why use a rigging plate on a tree climbing anchor?
faq.a: It separates connectors so each one sits in its own hole, which keeps the system tidy and avoids cross-loaded or binding carabiners.

faq.q: Can the X-Small plate be used for heavy rigging?
faq.a: It is meant for compact, lighter systems. Use components rated for heavy rigging forces when lowering big wood.

body.h: Using the PAW on tree jobs
p: Anchors get crowded fast: a climbing line, a backup, a pulley for a haul, a rope for the ground. Clipping all of that into one carabiner invites twisting and cross-loading. The PAW gives each piece its own hole so loads line up and the system is easy to check at a glance.

Common tree uses include a base anchor for a stationary rope system, a canopy anchor point, a rescue setup, or a hub for a small mechanical advantage. Load the plate along its intended axis and keep the system within the rating of the weakest part. Check Petzl's technical notice for the PAW medium.

The medium size gives enough holes for a busy anchor without getting bulky on the saddle. Spread connectors so they do not rub against one another, and use the top hole for the anchor sling and the lower holes for everything that hangs from it.

Before each use, look for cracks, deformation, and grooves worn by connectors, and retire the plate after a drop onto a hard surface from height. See other hardware in our blocks and hardware section.
Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard (ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions), be inspected before every climb, and be used only by trained climbers.

faq.q: What is a rigging plate used for in tree climbing?
faq.a: It gives every connector at an anchor its own attachment hole, keeping the system organized and loads aligned.

faq.q: Is the PAW medium good for SRS base anchors?
faq.a: Many climbers use rigging plates at base anchors. Follow Petzl's instructions and keep the setup within the rating of every component.

highlights: 2 in sheave for general rope work
Light and compact
Good for gear hauling and redirects
Useful in small mechanical advantage systems

p: A service pulley earns its spot by being handy. Send it up with a throw line to hang a gear-haul line, put it at the base to redirect a pull rope away from a hazard, or use it with a prusik to build a quick 3:1 for tensioning a line. Larger sheaves run more efficiently, but a 2 inch pulley is a good balance of size and weight for small jobs.
Keep the loads light. A service pulley is not a heavy rigging block, and it should not be used to catch falling wood. Check CMI's listed rating and rope range for this pulley.

Because it is cheap and light, many crews keep a couple in the truck alongside a few prusik loops and a spare length of rope, so there is always a simple haul system ready when a climber needs a saw, a pole tool, or a water bottle sent up.
Clean out sawdust and sap, spin the sheave to check for smooth rotation, and look over the side plates and axle for wear or damage. Find more pulleys in our rigging pulleys section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What is a service pulley used for?
faq.a: General rope work such as hauling gear, redirecting light lines, and building small mechanical advantage systems.

faq.q: Can I use it to lower wood?
faq.a: Not for catching falling wood. Use a rigging block and rope rated for those dynamic loads.

summary: The CMI stainless steel pulley for 5/8 inch rope is a heavy duty pulley built for the rough side of tree work, where gear gets dragged, dropped in the chips, and left in the rain. Stainless construction stands up to abrasion and corrosion better than aluminum, at the cost of some weight.
highlights: Stainless steel construction
Sized for 5/8 in rope
Resists wear and corrosion
Good for haul systems and redirects
Made by CMI

p: Steel and stainless pulleys trade weight for durability. On a ground-based setup, a redirect at the base of a tree, or a mechanical advantage system that lives in the truck, that extra weight does not matter much, and the toughness pays off in years of service. Rope running across grit and sap wears aluminum faster than steel.
Use it with rope inside CMI's listed diameter range and within the published rating. Remember that a redirect sees close to twice the line tension, so size the anchor and sling to match.

Stainless also holds up to the kind of treatment ground gear gets: being tossed in a truck box, run over by a chipper's feed line, or left in a wet rope bag overnight. Keep it for the ground and send lighter aluminum hardware up the tree, where every ounce on the saddle counts over a long day.
Check that the sheave turns freely, look for bent side plates or a worn axle, and clean out debris after muddy jobs. See other options in our rigging pulleys section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: Is stainless steel better than aluminum for pulleys?
faq.a: Stainless is heavier but tougher and more corrosion resistant. Aluminum is lighter for gear that goes up the tree.

faq.q: What rope does this pulley take?
faq.a: It is sized for 5/8 inch rope. Check CMI's listing for the exact diameter range.

A large sheave reduces how sharply the rope bends, which cuts rope wear and friction. Apply the stated working load guidance and keep the whole system within the weakest component's rating.

The aluminum frame keeps it light enough to carry up the tree, so it can serve as a canopy redirect for a pull line as well as a ground-level pulley. Clip it with a carabiner rated for the load and keep the gate closed and locked.
Before use, look over the side plates for cracks, check the axle and bushing for play, and make sure the sheave turns freely. See other pulleys in our rigging pulleys section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What does the 70 kN rating mean?
faq.a: It is the pulley's rated breaking strength. Working loads must be much lower; follow the manufacturer's working load guidance.

faq.q: Is a bushing pulley good for tree work?
faq.a: Yes for redirects, haul systems, and tensioning. Bushings are tough and simple, though slightly less efficient than ball bearings.

summary: The Rock Exotica Omni-Block 2.0 double is a two-sheave pulley with Rock Exotica's swiveling Omni-Block design, making it a natural fit for compact mechanical advantage systems. Arborists use it to tension lines, lift hung-up wood a few inches, and build tidy haul setups.

Mechanical advantage multiplies force, which also means it can overload an anchor or rope without anyone feeling it. Keep the system within the rating of the weakest component and check Rock Exotica's published ratings for this pulley.
Because the side plates open, you can load the pulley onto a rope that is already rigged, which saves time when you need to add a system partway through a job without untying anything.

Check the swivel for smooth rotation, spin each sheave, and look for cracks or wear on the side plates and attachment point. Keep it clear of grit and sap. See more pulleys in our rigging pulleys section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What is special about the Omni-Block?
faq.a: It swivels and the side plates open, so the pulley aligns with the load and can be loaded mid-rope.

Arborists use it as a redirect for a pull line, in a mechanical advantage system, or as part of a rescue kit. Check Rock Exotica's published ratings and rope range before planning a setup, and keep loads within the weakest link.

The opening side plates mean you can load the pulley onto a line that is already rigged, so you can add a redirect partway through a job without untying anything. It is a small detail that saves real time when a ground worker needs to change a pull angle quickly.

faq.a: It refers to the sheave size, about 2.6 inches, which is larger and more efficient than the 2.0 model.

faq.q: Single or double Omni-Block?
faq.a: A single suits redirects and simple haul systems. A double makes it easier to build higher-ratio mechanical advantage.

name: AMH Round Sling Hook
title: AMH Round Sling Hook for Rigging and Lifting
meta: The AMH round sling hook connects a round sling to a lifting line or crane hook with a wide, sling-friendly saddle. See how it is used and what to inspect.
tagline: A hook with a wide saddle shaped for round slings in lifting and rigging.
summary: The AMH round sling hook is a hook shaped to carry a round sling without pinching it, with a wide, smooth saddle that spreads the load across the sling body. Tree crews use hooks like this when lifting wood with a crane or connecting round slings in a rigging system.
highlights: Wide saddle shaped for round slings
Spreads load across the sling body
Used in crane and lifting setups
Fast connection for round slings
specs: Lifting and rigging with round slings

p: Round slings are strong and soft on wood, but they lose strength when pinched over a narrow hook or sharp edge. A round sling hook has a broader bearing surface so the sling sits flat and the load spreads across its full width.

On crane removals it connects slings to the load line, and in ground rigging it gives a quick attachment for a sling to a pulling or lifting system. Check the hook's marked working load limit and use it within that rating, with the latch closed and the load seated in the bowl, never on the tip.

Hooks speed up crane picks because the rigger can hang or release a sling quickly. That speed only helps if every pick is planned, every sling is sized to the piece, and the crane operator, rigger, and climber agree on signals before the first cut.

Before each lift, check for throat opening, twisting, cracks, nicks, and a damaged latch. Retire any hook that is bent or has an opened throat. See other hardware in our rings and other hardware section.
Crane and lifting work must follow the manufacturer's ratings, ANSI Z133, and the applicable crane and rigging standards, with qualified riggers and signal persons on site.

faq.q: Can I use a regular hook with a round sling?
faq.a: A narrow hook can pinch a round sling and reduce its strength. A hook made for round slings spreads the load properly.

faq.q: Where do I find the hook's rating?
faq.a: The working load limit should be marked on the hook. Do not use a hook without a legible rating.

name: FTC Fioris Ring
title: FTC Fioris Ring for Arborist Rigging
meta: The FTC Fioris ring is a rigging ring for arborist systems, used as a low-friction redirect, sling connector, or anchor point. See uses and inspection tips.
tagline: A rigging ring from FTC for redirects, sling connections, and anchors.
summary: The FTC Fioris ring is a rigging ring for tree work, used where a smooth, round bearing surface does a better job than a carabiner: as a low-friction redirect for light lines, a connection point for slings, or a retrievable anchor component. Rings have no gate to open, so they stay closed under any orientation.
highlights: Rigging ring with no gate to open
Smooth bearing surface for rope and slings
Useful as a light redirect or anchor point
Made by FTC

p: A ring is the simplest piece of hardware in the kit and one of the most useful. Spliced or girth-hitched to a sling, it becomes a smooth redirect for a pull line or light rigging line with less heat and wear than running over bark. Paired with another ring, it can form part of a retrievable friction saver setup.

Rings add friction compared with a pulley, so they are better for light loads or where some friction helps. Check FTC's listed rating and use the ring with rope and slings it is designed for. Do not use it to catch heavy, falling wood unless the manufacturer rates it for that.

Rings are also easy to inspect and hard to misuse, since there is no gate to leave open or cross-load. That simplicity is why so many climbers carry a spare or two on the saddle for whatever comes up during the day.
Look for grooves worn by rope, cracks, and sharp edges, and retire a ring with deep wear that could cut a sling or rope. See other hardware in our rings and other hardware section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: Ring or pulley for a redirect?
faq.a: A pulley is more efficient. A ring is simpler, lighter, and adds friction, which can be useful for light loads and some lowering setups.

faq.q: How do I know when a ring is worn out?
faq.a: Retire it when rope grooves get deep, sharp edges appear, or you see cracks or deformation.

name: Buckingham Port-A-Wrap Mini
title: Buckingham Port-A-Wrap Mini Lowering Device
meta: The Buckingham Port-A-Wrap Mini is a compact friction lowering device for light rigging on pruning and small removal jobs. See how it works and what to check.
tagline: A compact Port-A-Wrap for lowering light limbs and small wood.
summary: The Buckingham Port-A-Wrap Mini is a compact friction lowering device that lets a ground worker control light rigging loads on pruning and small removal jobs. Wrapping the rigging line around its barrel adds controllable friction, so pieces come down smoothly instead of running.
highlights: Compact friction lowering device
Adds controllable friction to a rigging line
For light limbs and small wood
Anchors to a tree with a sling
Made by Buckingham

p: Anchor the device to the base of a tree or another solid point with a sling, and take a number of wraps of the rigging line around the barrel. More wraps add friction; fewer wraps let the rope run more easily. The ground worker holds the tail and controls the descent of each piece, letting the rope run a little to soften the catch.

The Mini is made for lighter work: limbs over a roof, small wood, and pruning cuts on a light rigging line. Bigger wood and larger rope call for a full-size device. Check Buckingham's rope range and ratings before you choose it for a job.
Because it is small and light, the Mini is easy to carry into back yards and set up on a small tree or fence post that would not suit a larger device.

Keep hands and gloves clear of the wraps, wear gloves made for rope work, and watch for heat on long lowers. Inspect for grooves worn by rope, cracks, and damage at the anchor point. See full-size options in our lowering devices section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: How many wraps should I take on a Port-A-Wrap?
faq.a: It depends on the load and rope. Start with more friction than you think you need, follow Buckingham's guidance, and adjust as you learn the setup.

faq.q: Is the Mini enough for removals?
faq.a: For light limbs and small wood, yes. Heavier pieces need a larger lowering device and rope.

name: Rigging Rope Wrench (120 kg)
title: Rigging Rope Wrench 120 kg Lowering Device
meta: This rigging rope wrench is a friction lowering device rated to 120 kg for light rigging, letting you control small pieces and limbs from the tree or ground.
tagline: A friction lowering device for light rigging loads up to 120 kg.
summary: This rigging rope wrench is a friction device for controlling light rigging loads, rated up to 120 kg. It adds adjustable friction to the rigging line so a climber or ground worker can let limbs and small wood down smoothly without a full-size lowering device.
highlights: Friction device for light rigging
Rated for loads up to 120 kg
Controls limbs and small wood
Lighter and smaller than a full lowering device

body.h: Where a light rigging device fits
p: Not every rigging job needs a big Port-A-Wrap at the base of the tree. When you are lowering small limbs over a roof, pruning deadwood with a rope, or taking down a small ornamental, a compact friction device gives you control without the bulk. The 120 kg limit makes the boundary clear: this is for small, light pieces.

Remember that a falling piece can generate a force much higher than its weight. Keep pieces well under the limit, drop them short, and let the rope run a little on the catch. Use rope within the diameter range the maker lists, and follow their instructions for setup.

A small device like this is also handy as a backup in the truck, so a crew can run two light rigging lines at once on a pruning job. That lets one ground worker lower while another resets the second line and clears brush from the drop zone.
Before each use, check for rope grooves, cracks, and sharp edges, and look over the attachment points. See full-size lowering devices in our lowering devices section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What does the 120 kg limit cover?
faq.a: It is the stated maximum load for the device. Dynamic forces from a falling piece can exceed its weight, so keep pieces well under the limit.

faq.q: Can I use this rigging device for climbing?
faq.a: No. Use only climbing devices that are rated and sold for life support.

name: Stein RCW 3001 Lowering Device Complete
title: Stein RCW 3001 Lowering Device, Complete Kit
meta: The Stein RCW 3001 lowering device is a trunk-mounted rigging winch and friction system for controlled lowering and lifting on heavy arborist removals.
tagline: A trunk-mounted Stein rigging winch for controlled lowering and lifting.
summary: The Stein RCW 3001 lowering device is a trunk-mounted rigging control system that combines a friction drum for lowering with a winch for taking up slack and lifting. Sold complete, it gives a removal crew more control over heavy pieces than a plain friction device.
highlights: Trunk-mounted rigging control system
Friction drum for controlled lowering
Winch function for taking up slack and light lifts
Sold as a complete setup
Made by Stein

body.h: What the RCW adds to a rigging system
p: A friction device at the base lets you lower wood, but it cannot pull. The RCW mounts to the trunk, takes wraps of the rigging line like a friction device, and adds a winch so the ground crew can pre-tension the line, lift a piece clear of its cut, or take slack out before the catch. Pre-tensioning cuts the drop distance and the shock load.

It works best on heavy removals where control matters: wood over structures, big leaders, and pieces that need to be lifted a few inches before they swing. Use rope within Stein's listed diameter range and check Stein's ratings for the RCW 3001 before planning a lift.
Mounting the device on the trunk also means the ground worker stands off to the side of the drop zone instead of in front of it.

Mount it to a sound trunk following Stein's instructions, keep hands clear of the drum, and use the winch handle only as directed. Inspect the strap, drum, winch, and fasteners before every job. See other options in our lowering devices section.

Rigging forces are dynamic and can be several times the weight of the piece. Follow the manufacturer's ratings and ANSI Z133, inspect every component before the job, and keep rigging work to trained crews.

faq.q: What is the difference between the RCW and a Port-A-Wrap?
faq.a: Both add friction for lowering, but the RCW also has a winch so the crew can tension the line and lift pieces slightly.

faq.q: Does the RCW need a dedicated anchor tree?
faq.a: It mounts to a trunk, often the tree being removed or a nearby sound tree. Follow Stein's mounting instructions.
